text:
Genesis 22 rewards the reader who attends to what is wanting in it. Sarah is nowhere in the chapter, and the book announces her death in the verse immediately following. The scene implies, though it does not declare, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants; Isaac is not named in that return. The text turns away at the precise point at which a lesser story would linger. Silence here is more than absence; it is testimony.

It may be answered that the chapter only follows the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains; and perhaps, in some sense, this may be true. Yet the narrator elsewhere reports what characters feel. Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence of this passage is deliberate. The text knows what it is doing. Restraint, in this narrative voice, is a kind of accusation.
